prompt: `exp.run` calls `torch.manual_seed(seed)` just before building the network. What does that line fix?
hint: Look at what is drawn from PyTorch's generator right after it.

choices.text: Which images go into the training set
choices.why: The split comes from `digits.load(seed=0)`, a separate seed that this lesson never changes.

choices.text: The starting weights
choices.why: Right. `build` draws them from the generator the seed has just reset.

choices.text: The learning rate the optimiser starts from
choices.why: The rate is a setting in the config, never drawn at random.

choices.text: Whether the run gives the same accuracy on any computer
choices.why: A seed repeats a run on the same machine and libraries; across machines the arithmetic can differ.

prompt: `seeds.py` trained seed 0 twice and printed `True` for every weight being equal. What does that show?
hint: `torch.equal` compares to the last bit.

choices.text: That seed 0 is the best seed for this configuration
choices.why: Seed 0 was one draw among many; the next section shows others doing better.

choices.text: That the network has stopped learning after ten epochs
choices.why: Two runs being equal says nothing about whether either kept improving.

choices.text: That every random choice in training came from the seed
choices.why: Right. If anything had been left unseeded, some weight would have differed.

choices.text: That the accuracy, 0.9167, is the accuracy of the configuration
choices.why: It is the accuracy of one seed. The configuration's is a range.

prompt: A colleague's training script calls `torch.manual_seed(0)` at the top, but shuffles the batches with `random.shuffle` from Python's own library. Run twice, it gives two different accuracies. Why?
hint: How many generators are in that program?

choices.text: Python's `random` has its own generator, which nothing seeded
choices.why: Right. Each generator needs its own seed; here the batch order is still drawn fresh every run.

choices.text: `manual_seed` only works on a graphics card
choices.why: It fixed the weights on the processor in `seeds.py`.

choices.text: Seed 0 is reserved and gives a random start
choices.why: Seed 0 repeated itself to the last bit in this lesson.

choices.text: Shuffling changes nothing, so the difference is the threads
choices.why: Batch order is one of the three random things the lesson lists, and it moves the result.

prompt: `spread.py` printed 329 correct images for its worst seed and 333 for its best. How many images apart were the best and worst runs?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: Why does validation accuracy on these digits move in steps of about 0.0028?
hint: Count the validation set.

choices.text: Because `float32` cannot hold finer values
choices.why: `float32` holds far finer differences; the step comes from counting images.

choices.text: One image is 1/360 of the set
choices.why: Right. Accuracy is a count of correct images divided by 360, so it moves one image at a time.

choices.text: The learning rate sets the size of every change
choices.why: The rate moves weights, not the granularity of a count.

choices.text: `loop.evaluate` rounds to three decimals
choices.why: It returns the full number; only the printing rounds.

prompt: A team reports that a new configuration reached 0.94 validation accuracy, from one run, against 0.92 for the old one, also from one run. What is the first thing to ask?
hint: What else differs between two single runs?

choices.text: Whether 0.94 was computed with `float64`
choices.why: Precision does not move accuracy by two points.

choices.text: Which of the two ran on more threads
choices.why: Threads change last digits; the larger question is the seed.

choices.text: Whether the test set agrees
choices.why: Reading test to decide between them would spend it on a choice.

choices.text: How much each configuration moves across seeds
choices.why: Right. Until the spread is known, two points may be two seeds rather than two settings.

prompt: Why does `track.py` append one JSON line per run instead of keeping a single JSON array?
hint: What happens to the file if a run crashes while writing?

choices.text: JSON arrays cannot hold dictionaries
choices.why: They can; the trouble is having to rewrite the whole file.

choices.text: Appending never rewrites earlier runs, so a crash cannot lose them
choices.why: Right. An array has to be read and rewritten whole on every run.

choices.text: It makes the file smaller
choices.why: The size is about the same; what changes is how it is written.

choices.text: PyTorch can only read JSON Lines
choices.why: PyTorch never reads `runs.jsonl`; `report.py` reads it with the `json` module.

prompt: A record says `"commit": "…", "dirty": true`. What does it tell you about the code that produced the number?
hint: What does `git status --porcelain` report?

choices.text: It is exactly the named commit
choices.why: That is what `false` would say.

choices.text: The commit failed and the run is invalid
choices.why: The commit exists; the files on disk differed from it when the run started.

choices.text: It is the named commit plus edits nobody saved in git
choices.why: Right, and those edits cannot be recovered from the record, so the run cannot be repeated.

choices.text: The data changed since the last run
choices.why: The data has its own fingerprint in `data`; `dirty` is only about the code.

prompt: Put in order what makes a run that somebody else can repeat.
hint: The record names the commit, so the commit comes before the run.
items: Run with a seed, from the command line
Append the record, then read the report

prompt: Two runs have the same config, seed, commit and library versions, and different accuracies. `data.sha256` differs between them. What most likely happened?
hint: What does the fingerprint hash?

choices.text: A different number of threads
choices.why: Threads are recorded separately and do not change the data's bytes.

choices.text: The training images were not the same bytes
choices.why: Right. A different split seed, or a data set that changed, changes the hash with the code untouched.

choices.text: Somebody edited `exp.py` without committing
choices.why: That would show as `dirty: true`, and leave the data's hash alone.

choices.text: The seed was ignored
choices.why: A seed that was ignored changes weights, not the bytes of the training set.

prompt: On seed 0, the 64-unit layer beat the 32-unit one, 0.9194 to 0.9167. What did five seeds say?
hint: Compare the means with the standard deviations.

choices.text: The wider layer is better by about a point
choices.why: The means were 0.9200 and 0.9211: no point, and in the other direction.

choices.text: No measurable difference
choices.why: Right. The means differ by less than half an image, well inside the spread.

choices.text: The wider layer is worse, so the narrow one should be kept for its accuracy
choices.why: A gap of 0.0011 against a spread near 0.006 shows no difference either way.

choices.text: Seed 0 is the fair seed to compare on
choices.why: No seed is fairer than another; seed 4 said the opposite of seed 0.

prompt: Why does `report.py` group runs by configuration and commit, not by configuration alone?
hint: What else can change a result with the settings untouched?

choices.text: Git refuses to read a file with two commits in it
choices.why: `report.py` reads JSON and never calls git.

choices.text: So that seeds are not counted twice
choices.why: That is done by keying each group on the seed, a separate step.

choices.text: The same settings on different code are a different experiment
choices.why: Right. Mixing commits would average two programs as if they were one.

choices.text: Dirty runs have no commit
choices.why: They do have one; they are left out for having edits on top of it.

prompt: Configuration A scores 0.930, 0.925, 0.935, 0.928, 0.932 over five seeds, and B scores 0.931, 0.940, 0.926, 0.938, 0.929 on the same seeds. What can you conclude?
hint: Do the ranges overlap?

choices.text: B is better, because its best run is the highest of all
choices.why: One high run is the single-seed comparison again, with a different seed.

choices.text: Not enough: the ranges overlap almost entirely
choices.why: Right. A's worst, 0.925, and B's worst, 0.926, sit together; more seeds are the next step.

choices.text: A is better, because its runs vary less
choices.why: A smaller spread is not a higher accuracy.

choices.text: B is better, so read the test set to confirm it
choices.why: Using the test set to decide a comparison spends it on a choice.

prompt: Floating-point addition rounds after every step, so changing the ___ of a sum can change its result.
hint: `order.py` added the same three numbers in two groupings.

prompt: In `threads.py`, one thread and four gave identical weights. Why does `track.py` record the number of threads anyway?
hint: What did `order.py` show for a million numbers?

choices.text: Because more threads give a higher accuracy
choices.why: Threads change speed and rounding, not what the network can learn.

choices.text: Because PyTorch ignores the seed on four threads
choices.why: The seed held on four threads, as the identical weights show.

choices.text: A larger network's sums are split by thread, and their rounding differs
choices.why: Right. The million-number sum changed on four threads, and over many steps that grows.

choices.text: Because a run on one thread cannot be repeated
choices.why: One thread is the easiest case to repeat.

prompt: A run on a graphics card with a fixed seed gives 0.9611, then 0.9583 on the next try, on the same machine. Which change is aimed at exactly that?
hint: Same machine, same seed: what is still free to vary?

choices.text: A different seed for each run
choices.why: That adds variation; it does not remove the one that is there.

choices.text: Recording the library versions
choices.why: Worth doing, but the versions were the same on both tries.

choices.text: More epochs, so both runs converge to the same point
choices.why: Training longer does not bring two different paths to one point.

choices.text: `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and the settings beside it
choices.why: Right. On a card some operations add in the order the hardware finishes, and these settings forbid that, at a cost in speed.

prompt: Match each tool to what the lesson says about it.
hint: One is a file, one is hosted, one is open source, one is a viewer.

pairs.right: one line per run, enough for one person and one machine
open source, on your own machine or a team server
a hosted service that keeps the runs on its servers
draws curves, and leaves the config and code version to you

prompt: Which of these does moving from `runs.jsonl` to a tracking tool give you, according to the lesson?
hint: The tools sell what grows around the record.

choices.text: Runs that no longer need a seed
choices.why: Every tool records the seed you give it; none removes the need for one.

choices.text: Plots of many runs, shared between people and machines
choices.why: Right. The record is the same idea; the tools add viewing, sharing and storage.

choices.text: A decision on which configuration is better
choices.why: The comparison against the spread is still yours to make.

choices.text: Determinism on a graphics card
choices.why: That comes from PyTorch's settings, not from the tracker.

prompt: Which of these did this lesson's runs show? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each against a transcript.

choices.text: Seed 0 run twice gave identical weights
choices.why: Yes: `every weight equal to the first run's: True`.

choices.text: The 64-unit layer beat the 32-unit one on every seed
choices.why: No: it won on seed 0 and lost on seed 4.

choices.text: A learning rate of 0.05 beat 0.01 on every seed
choices.why: Yes: its worst seed, 0.9500, beat the other configurations' best.

choices.text: A sum of a million numbers changed with the number of threads
choices.why: Yes: four threads gave different last digits from one or two.

choices.text: A run with uncommitted edits was counted in the report
choices.why: No: `left out: 1 run(s) from uncommitted code`.

prompt: You want to know whether adding dropout helps this network. Which plan follows the lesson?
hint: Seeds, commit, validation, test.

choices.text: Run each version once on seed 0 and keep the higher
choices.why: That compares one seed; the 64-unit layer looked better that way and was not.

choices.text: Commit, run both on the same five seeds, compare on validation
choices.why: Right, and only then read the test set, once, for the one you chose.

choices.text: Edit `exp.py`, run five seeds without committing, then commit the winner
choices.why: Those runs are dirty: the record cannot say which code produced them.

choices.text: Compare both on the test set, which is the honest measure
choices.why: Test is for reporting a choice already made; choosing on it overstates the result.
